## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a8-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Duration</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="battery-duration">Energy ÷ power</span>: how long a store gives full power. 4,000 MWh at 1,000 MW is 4 hours.</dd>
<dt>Round trip</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="round-trip-efficiency">What comes back</span> of 1 MWh put in: 83% for the battery, 31% for hydrogen.</dd>
<dt>Heat losses</dt><dd>A hot store cools whether or not it is used, a <span class="lx-term" data-term="standing-loss">standing loss</span>: 2% a day here.</dd>
<dt>Endurance</dt><dd>In the calm week the battery covers 21% of the shortfall, the hydrogen store 92%.</dd>
<dt>Power still matters</dt><dd>In 23 hours the gap tops firm output plus 1,000 MW: no 1,000 MW store can close it.</dd>
<dt>Cost per MWh delivered</dt><dd>Yearly cost ÷ MWh delivered a year: the fewer the cycles, the more each MWh carries.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the cost per MWh delivered depends on cycles</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The formula.** Cost per MWh delivered = capital recovery × installed cost ÷ (cycles a year × duration), plus the charging price ÷ round trip.
- **The battery.** At 250 cycles a year and \$20/MWh charging power, 4 hours at \$1,540 per kW gives \$132 of capital and \$24 of charging: \$156 per MWh.
- **Hydrogen.** A 24-hour hydrogen store at 31% needs 24 + 24 ÷ 0.31 = 101 hours a cycle, so at most 86 cycles a year: \$149 per MWh at best, \$65 of it charging.
- **Left out.** Fixed upkeep adds under a quarter to the capital for pumped hydro and hydrogen (\$28.19 and \$23.90 per kW-year); the report gives no battery figure at this size.
- **Longer hydrogen stores** add mostly cavern, at \$5.82 per kWh in the report: energy capacity is cheap, the converters are not.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The week as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For each hour $t = 0 \dots 167$ (one hour each, so MW over the hour is MWh), with a store of power $P$, energy $E$, round trip $\eta$ and standing loss $\lambda$ per hour:

$$\min \sum_t \big(V + \tau\,(168 - t)\big)\,u_t + \delta \sum_t d_t$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t + u_t - s_t - c_t + d_t &= g_t && \text{(balance)}\\
e_t = (1-\lambda)\,e_{t-1} + \eta\,c_t - d_t, \quad e_{-1} &= E && \text{(level; starts full)}\\
0 \le f_t \le 1{,}000, \quad 0 \le s_t \le w_t + \sigma_t, \quad 0 \le c_t, d_t \le P, \quad 0 \le e_t &\le E, \quad u_t \ge 0 && \text{(limits)}
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $g_t$ | the gap: demand minus wind and sun | MW |
| $f_t$ | firm (gas) output | MW |
| $u_t$, $s_t$ | unserved demand, spilled wind and sun | MW |
| $c_t$, $d_t$ | charging and discharging | MW |
| $e_t$ | energy held at the end of hour $t$ | MWh |
| $\lambda$ | standing loss: $1 - 0.98^{1/24}$ for 2% a day | per hour |
| $V$, $\tau$, $\delta$ | \$10,000 per MWh unserved; tie rule \$0.01 per MWh per hour; \$0.001 per MWh discharged | \$/MWh |

- **Tie rule, stated in advance.** Many schedules leave the same MWh unserved. $\tau$ pushes shortfalls late and $\delta$ uses firm output before the store; neither changes the least unserved energy, the only number the page reads.
- **One of the best schedules.** The dashed line in step 5 is the one this tie rule picks; others leave the same MWh unserved.
- **Next.** [M4](m04-storage-multienergy.html) adds conversion between carriers; [M3](m03-capacity-expansion.html) links a store across representative weeks of a whole year.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The rest of the year: whether a store refills before the next calm spell needs the whole year in order (<a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a>).</li>
<li>Adequacy: many weather years and plant outages, judged by a criterion such as a loss-of-load expectation (A5, upcoming).</li>
<li>Building the stores: here each is given, at 1,000 MW; choosing sizes is capacity expansion (<a href="13-capstone.html">lesson 13</a>, M3).</li>
<li>Wires: the Plains Grid is one node with no limits on its lines.</li>
<li>Wear, fixed upkeep and replacements in the costs; costs differ by site and change over time.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a8-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="energy" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A store that holds more energy than the week's shortfall can always cover the week.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The hydrogen store holds 168,000 MWh against a 47,733 MWh shortfall, yet leaves 4,009 MWh unserved: in 23 hours the gap tops firm output plus its 1,000 MW.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="week" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If a store gets a grid through its calmest week, the grid is <span class="lx-term" data-term="resource-adequacy">adequate</span>.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A week shows endurance. Adequacy needs many weather years and plant outages, and the store must also refill in time for the next calm spell.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cheap" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The store with the lowest installed cost per kWh delivers the cheapest MWh.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Hydrogen has the lowest installed cost per kWh ($126, against $263 for pumped hydro and $385 for the battery). At 250 cycles a year pumped hydro delivers the cheapest MWh, $71; hydrogen, capped at 86 cycles, $149.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a8">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dur" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A pumped storage plant is rated 400 MW and 3,200 MWh. What is its duration?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">0.125 hours</li><li data-value="b">3,600 hours</li><li data-value="c">8 hours</li><li data-value="d">2,800 hours</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>8 hours: 3,200 MWh ÷ 400 MW. 0.125 is the ratio upside down; 3,600 and 2,800 add or subtract MW and MWh, which have different units.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="back" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">You put 10 MWh into the lesson's heat store (50% round trip, 2% a day) and take it out 5 days later. About how much comes back?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">5.0 MWh</li><li data-value="b">4.5 MWh</li><li data-value="c">9.0 MWh</li><li data-value="d">4.0 MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 4.5 MWh: 10 × 0.50 × 0.98<sup>5</sup> = 4.52. 5.0 forgets the heat losses; 9.0 forgets the round trip; 4.0 takes 2% of the original 10 MWh off each day, not 2% of what is left.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
